question: For several months, a number of coastal regions in southern Europe – including Puglia, Sardinia, the Balearic Islands and the Setúbal region of Portugal – have seen people mobilising against tourist complex mega-projects that threaten sensitive coastal ecosystems, echoing the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ in Albania.

These projects raise concerns about protecting biodiversity, land take, privatisation of the coast and land grabbing to the benefit of private interests. In several Member States, public authorities are watering down environmental protections to facilitate such projects, such as in Mallorca, or relying on derogation arrangements, such as special economic zones in Italy.
This development calls into question compliance with EU law on nature protection, particularly when it concerns protected natural areas. 1.
Does the Commission consider authorising major tourism projects in protected natural areas to be in compliance with obligations under EU nature protection legislation?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that EU nature protection legislation is applied when national or regional authorities relax environmental protections in order to facilitate the implementation of major tourism projects?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.10.2026) The Commission published on 14 July 2026 a new guidance document on Natura 2000 and sustainable tourism1, to help Member States and stakeholders reconcile nature protection with socio-economic development.
The guidance provides a framework to address tourism pressures by assessing carrying capacity, identifying impacts and providing appropriate management measures.

EU nature protection legislation does not automatically exclude tourism or other economic activities in or around Natura 2000 sites designated under the Birds2 and Habitats3 Directives4, provided they do not cause deterioration of habitats, or significant disturbance of species (Article 6 (2) of the Habitats Directive) for which the sites were designated.

Where a plan or project is likely to significantly affect a Natura 2000 site, it must undergo an appropriate assessment under Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive and may be authorised only where, taking account of cumulative effects, it has been ascertained that it will not adversely affect the integrity of the site.

Accordingly, tourism projects in protected areas can be compatible with EU nature protection legislation only where all applicable requirements of that legislations are fully complied with. Member States remain responsible for land-use and tourism planning, but measures designed to facilitate investment or development cannot exempt projects from applicable EU environmental requirements.

In particular, regulatory or economic regimes that relax national safeguards cannot circumvent the obligations arising under EU environmental legislation, including requirements concerning the protection of birds, habitats, water and marine resources, and environmental impact assessment.

1 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/4cc63772-80c4-11f1-bf5e-01aa75ed71a1/language-en. 2 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the

conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25. 3 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 4 Natura 2000 Viewer https://natura2000.eea.europa.eu/ and Natura 2000 network https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/natura-2000_en.
